DOCUMENT:
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Total | | £174,000" -- The cost lines sum to £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = £164,000, not £174,000. The growth bid is overstated by £10,000.
2. [inconsistency] at: "The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand" -- Section 3 states the Ashgrove pilot ran from October 2025 to March 2026, i.e. six months; the conclusion calls it a twelve-month pilot.
3. [misread_evidence] at: "Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level" -- Table 1 shows 21 visits per hour in the new weekday evening slot versus 46 and 58 in weekday daytime slots, i.e. less than half the daytime level. The text misstates the table, and the claim of strong evening demand rests on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours budget justification

The bid has a clear structure and a good evidence base: a real pilot, a survey finding, and a link to the Council Plan. But it has an arithmetic error in the headline figure, and several claims in the conclusion and in your description aren't supported by the document's own numbers. Finance or scrutiny Members are likely to spot these, so they're worth fixing before submission.

## Must fix

**1. The costs don't sum to £174,000.**
Table 2 gives £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = **£164,000**. Either a line is missing (worth about £10,000) or the total is wrong. The headline figure appears in sections 1 and 8 and in the cost-per-visit calculation, so it needs resolving first.

**2. Evening use is not "close to daytime levels."**
Table 1 shows evening visits at **21 per hour**, against 46–58 on weekday daytimes. That is roughly 35–45% of daytime use. Section 3's statement that evening visits "averaged close to the weekday daytime level" is contradicted by the table directly above it. The same claim appears in the conclusion and in your summary. Sunday (52 per hour) does match daytime levels, and that is the real headline.

A more defensible framing would be: "Sunday use matched weekday daytime levels. Evening use was lower but sustained, and supported a fully booked job club." The evening figures could also justify asking whether two evenings are needed, or whether one evening plus Sunday would give better value.

**3. The pilot ran for six months, not twelve.**
October 2025 to March 2026 is six months. The conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot."

## Should address

**4. The utilities figure is extrapolated from winter months.**
Utilities are "based on actual additional costs… scaled to a full year." Your summary says they come from "actual pilot spend rather than estimates," but scaling a winter-only pilot to a full year is an estimate. Winter heating and lighting will likely overstate the annual cost. That's a cautious bias, but say so.

**5. Applying Ashgrove's rates to all five branches is undercut by the bid itself.**
The 84,000-visit figure is correct arithmetic at Ashgrove rates: (6×21 + 4×52) × 50 weeks × 5 branches ≈ 83,500. But section 7 says Ashgrove is the busiest branch and the others may see lower demand. So the value-for-money case rests on a best-case assumption. Consider:
- adding a sensitivity line, such as cost per visit if the other four branches achieve 60% of Ashgrove's usage, or
- scaling each branch by its current daytime footfall relative to Ashgrove.

**6. Some "additional" visits may be displaced visits.**
Some evening and Sunday visitors may previously have come in on weekdays or Saturdays. If you have Ashgrove's daytime figures from before the pilot, show that they held up. That would considerably strengthen the claim that demand is new.

**7. The cost-per-visit comparison isn't like-for-like.**
£2 per visit is a marginal cost (staff plus utilities only). The borough's £3.40 average includes buildings, stock, management and IT. The comparison flatters the bid. Either note this or drop the comparison.

**8. The membership increase isn't clearly caused by the extended hours.**
1,140 vs 690 is a 65% rise, so "about two-thirds" is fair. But there's no control: the other four branches over the same period would show whether membership rose borough-wide. Also, were the new members actually signing up during the extended hours?

**9. The self-service comparison doesn't show it would cost more.**
Your summary says the bid explains why self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The document doesn't actually demonstrate that, and the figures suggest the opposite over time:
- Cutting staffing by two-thirds saves about £83,000 a year.
- Building works are about £300,000 one-off (5 × £60,000), which is capital, not revenue.
- Payback is therefore under four years.

The stronger and more honest argument is the one you already make about service quality: self-service can't support the job club and family activities. Present the numbers transparently and rest the case on that. Also explain why self-service would cut staffing by two-thirds rather than entirely.

## Minor points

- **Staffing rate.** One blended £24.80 rate includes a Sunday enhancement, but Sundays are only 4 of the 10 hours. State how the blend was built, and whether evenings attract an enhancement too.
- **Opening and closing time.** Two staff for exactly the opening hours leaves no time for opening up and closing down. Check whether 15–30 minutes per session should be added.
- **Kiosk line.** It is labelled as both "upgrades" and "maintenance contract," and it's unclear why staffed opening needs it. Clarify.
- **Current status at Ashgrove.** Say what happened after March 2026: did the extended hours stop? Members will ask.
- **Anecdotal evidence.** "Particularly popular with families" would be stronger with a figure, such as the share of Sunday visitors who were children or family groups, or attendance at family events.

## Summary

The core case is credible. Sunday demand and the job club are genuinely persuasive, and the survey finding is strong. But the total doesn't add up, the evening claim contradicts the bid's own table, and the pilot length is misstated. These are the kinds of errors that cause a scrutiny panel to distrust everything else in a paper. Fix those three, add a cautious demand scenario, and present the self-service comparison accurately, and the bid will be considerably harder to challenge.
